label: Opus 4.8
rationale: Anchored on the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT), where by 2100 median forecasts for total catastrophe (≥10% deaths) were ~9% (superforecasters) to 20% (experts) and total extinction ~1-6%; I use blended ~15% and ~5.5%. Domain splits: nuclear catastrophic 4-8%/extinction 0.07-0.55%, AI extinction 0.38% (super) to several % (experts), engineered pathogen catastrophe low single digits. Lower thresholds (≥1k, ≥100k) are far more probable and near-certain at the "all causes" level given routine disasters/pandemics/conflicts; higher thresholds fall steeply following power-law severity distributions. Time scaling: near-zero incremental risk to 2030 (AGI/engineered-bio capabilities still maturing, no current nuclear war), rising sharply 2050-2100 as AI capability, biotech democratization, and nuclear arms-race trends (SIPRI 2025) compound. All cells enforce monotonicity across horizons and thresholds, and specific causes stay below the all-causes envelope; Q31 (single-event ≥1k nuclear, 2030 only) set at 10% reflecting elevated near-term risk with no further horizon growth as specified. Extinction is dominated by AI in the long run, with bio and nuclear contributing less, summing to the total-extinction figure.

rationale: Anchored on the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT), where by 2100 median forecasts for total catastrophe (≥10% deaths) were ~9% (superforecasters) to 20% (experts) and total extinction ~1-6%; I use blended ~15% and ~5.5%. Domain splits: nuclear catastrophic 4-8%/extinction 0.07-0.55%, AI extinction 0.38% (super) to several % (experts), engineered pathogen catastrophe low single digits. Lower thresholds (≥1k, ≥100k) are far more probable and near-certain at the "all causes" level given routine disasters/pandemics/conflicts; higher thresholds fall steeply following power-law severity distributions. Time scaling: near-zero incremental risk to 2030 (AGI/engineered-bio capabilities still maturing, no current nuclear war), rising sharply 2050-2100 as AI capability, biotech democratization, and nuclear arms-race trends (SIPRI 2025) compound. All cells enforce monotonicity across horizons and thresholds, and specific causes stay below the all-causes envelope; Q31 (single-event ≥1k nuclear, 2030 only) set at 10% reflecting elevated near-term risk with no further horizon growth as specified. Extinction is dominated by AI in the long run, with bio and nuclear contributing less, summing to the total-extinction figure.

label: GPT-5.5
rationale: I started from historical base rates: thousand-death disasters are common, 100k-death events occur several times per century, million-plus events are dominated by pandemics, wars and famine, while billion-death and extinction scenarios have no direct modern base rate and require model-based tail judgments. Current evidence raises the near-term nuclear-use risk above Cold-War-average peacetime levels because multiple nuclear-armed crises persist, but I keep nuclear extinction very low because even large exchanges are unlikely to reduce humanity below 5,000. For bio, I assign low near-term but rising long-run risk because deliberate contagious bioweapon history is sparse, while synthetic biology and AI-enabled design are lowering barriers and increasing possible severity. For AI, I put substantial century-scale tail risk, informed by expert concern and fast capability progress, but discount the highest expert-survey p(doom) numbers for definitional strictness, governance/defense responses, and the need for deaths within the specified windows. The all-cause ladder is set as a coherent envelope over the specific causes, adding natural pandemics, geophysical disasters, climate/famine and other wars, and all entries were checked for monotonicity across time and severity.

Ragnarök Question Series: if a global biological catastrophe occurs, will it reduce the human population by 95% or more?
If there is a biotechnological or bioengineered organism catastrophe this century, when will it happen?
By five years after AGI, will an engineered pandemic have infected one billion people?

label: GPT-5.5
rationale: I started from historical base rates: thousand-death disasters are common, 100k-death events occur several times per century, million-plus events are dominated by pandemics, wars and famine, while billion-death and extinction scenarios have no direct modern base rate and require model-based tail judgments. Current evidence raises the near-term nuclear-use risk above Cold-War-average peacetime levels because multiple nuclear-armed crises persist, but I keep nuclear extinction very low because even large exchanges are unlikely to reduce humanity below 5,000. For bio, I assign low near-term but rising long-run risk because deliberate contagious bioweapon history is sparse, while synthetic biology and AI-enabled design are lowering barriers and increasing possible severity. For AI, I put substantial century-scale tail risk, informed by expert concern and fast capability progress, but discount the highest expert-survey p(doom) numbers for definitional strictness, governance/defense responses, and the need for deaths within the specified windows. The all-cause ladder is set as a coherent envelope over the specific causes, adding natural pandemics, geophysical disasters, climate/famine and other wars, and all entries were checked for monotonicity across time and severity.

Current evidence raises the near-term nuclear-use risk above Cold-War-average peacetime levels because multiple nuclear-armed crises persist, but I keep nuclear extinction very low because even large exchanges are unlikely to reduce humanity below 5,000. For bio, I assign low near-term but rising long-run risk because deliberate contagious bioweapon history is sparse, while synthetic biology and AI-enabled design are lowering barriers and increasing possible severity. For AI, I put substantial century-scale tail risk, informed by expert concern and fast capability progress, but discount the highest expert-survey p(doom) numbers for definitional strictness, governance/defense responses, and the need for deaths within the specified windows. The all-cause ladder is set as a coherent envelope over the specific causes, adding natural pandemics, geophysical disasters, climate/famine and other wars, and all entries were checked for monotonicity across time and severity.

rationale: Anchored on the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) medians — superforecasters gave ~9% total catastrophe and ~1% extinction by 2100, domain experts ~20% and ~6% — I place estimates between the two, tilted toward superforecasters but adjusted upward for AI given capability acceleration since 2022 (agentic systems, military AI targeting, demonstrated bio/cyber uplift). Low thresholds resolve from base rates: single events killing 100k+ occur roughly once a decade (2004 tsunami, Haiti 2010, COVID, major wars), so total ladders at ≥100k–≥1M are dominated by pandemics and conflict, while ≥100M+ outcomes require nuclear exchange with winter effects, an engineered pandemic, or AI-driven catastrophe. Bioweapon-actor questions reflect a near-zero historical base rate of mass-casualty contagious-agent attacks, offset by rising accessibility of synthesis and AI uplift over decades. Nuclear numbers reflect elevated but non-crisis tensions (Ukraine, South Asia, Taiwan), with ~3-4% odds of any use killing 1,000+ by 2030 and heavy discounting from use to escalation to global-scale mortality; nuclear extinction is kept very low (winter unlikely to kill literally everyone), consistent with XPT nuclear-expert and superforecaster views. All ladders are monotonic in threshold and horizon, cause-specific values never exceed all-cause values, and narrower actor/route questions sit below their containing ladders.

Stages 2-4 of the XPT tournament ask participants to engage in constructive debates, adversarial collaboration style (Kahneman, 2011), in which each side shares its best arguments and makes good faith efforts to understand the other side’s arguments. [...] Table 1 provides the median forecast of XPT participants on whether AI, use of bioweapons, nuclear war, or non-anthropogenic risks will, by 2100, cause a ”catastrophe,” killing within a five-year period more than 10% of humans alive at the beginning of that period. We separately asked experts about five different types of risk. Relative to generalists, specialists expressed greater concern about both catastrophic and existential risk across the board, with the differences most pronounced on [...] human extinction, contributing about 10% to his cumulative estimate of a 16% probability of extinction. Even two of the three “Godfathers of AI”, Geoffrey Hinton and Yoshua Bengio, have expressed serious concern about the existential risks posed by AI (D’Agostino, 2023).

label: Fable 5
rationale: Anchored on the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) medians — superforecasters gave ~9% total catastrophe and ~1% extinction by 2100, domain experts ~20% and ~6% — I place estimates between the two, tilted toward superforecasters but adjusted upward for AI given capability acceleration since 2022 (agentic systems, military AI targeting, demonstrated bio/cyber uplift). Low thresholds resolve from base rates: single events killing 100k+ occur roughly once a decade (2004 tsunami, Haiti 2010, COVID, major wars), so total ladders at ≥100k–≥1M are dominated by pandemics and conflict, while ≥100M+ outcomes require nuclear exchange with winter effects, an engineered pandemic, or AI-driven catastrophe. Bioweapon-actor questions reflect a near-zero historical base rate of mass-casualty contagious-agent attacks, offset by rising accessibility of synthesis and AI uplift over decades. Nuclear numbers reflect elevated but non-crisis tensions (Ukraine, South Asia, Taiwan), with ~3-4% odds of any use killing 1,000+ by 2030 and heavy discounting from use to escalation to global-scale mortality; nuclear extinction is kept very low (winter unlikely to kill literally everyone), consistent with XPT nuclear-expert and superforecaster views. All ladders are monotonic in threshold and horizon, cause-specific values never exceed all-cause values, and narrower actor/route questions sit below their containing ladders.

Low thresholds resolve from base rates: single events killing 100k+ occur roughly once a decade (2004 tsunami, Haiti 2010, COVID, major wars), so total ladders at ≥100k–≥1M are dominated by pandemics and conflict, while ≥100M+ outcomes require nuclear exchange with winter effects, an engineered pandemic, or AI-driven catastrophe. Bioweapon-actor questions reflect a near-zero historical base rate of mass-casualty contagious-agent attacks, offset by rising accessibility of synthesis and AI uplift over decades. Nuclear numbers reflect elevated but non-crisis tensions (Ukraine, South Asia, Taiwan), with ~3-4% odds of any use killing 1,000+ by 2030 and heavy discounting from use to escalation to global-scale mortality; nuclear extinction is kept very low (winter unlikely to kill literally everyone), consistent with XPT nuclear-expert and superforecaster views. All ladders are monotonic in threshold and horizon, cause-specific values never exceed all-cause values, and narrower actor/route questions sit below their containing ladders.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: Forecasts are grounded in base rates of natural and anthropogenic catastrophes, adjusted for emerging technological risks, and heavily informed by the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) results. Total extinction risk by 2100 is estimated at 2.5%, reflecting a blend of superforecaster (1%) and expert (6%) consensus, with AI (1.5%) as the primary driver, followed by engineered pandemics (0.2%) and nuclear war (0.05%). Lower severity thresholds (e.g., ≥1k, ≥100k) are dominated by natural disasters and conventional conflicts, approaching 100% for 'Total' risk over longer horizons. AI risk scales steeply over time as capabilities advance, while nuclear risk remains relatively flat due to established deterrence mechanisms. Biological risks are elevated by the increasing accessibility of genetic engineering, though state and non-state actor capabilities are differentiated. All probabilities strictly adhere to logical constraints: non-decreasing over time, non-increasing with severity, and respecting subset/superset relationships across causes and thresholds.

# Elon Musk predicts smarter-than-humans AI in 2 years. The CEO of China's Baidu says it's 10 years away

thumbnail

In this article

PARIS — Robin Li, CEO of one of China's biggest tech firms Baidu, said artificial intelligence that is smarter than humans is more than 10 years away, even as industry staple Elon Musk predicts it will emerge very soon.

Artificial general intelligence, or AGI, broadly relates to AI that is as smart or smarter than humans. [...] Tesla boss Musk said this year that AGI would likely be available by 2026. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said in January that AGI could be developed in the "reasonably close-ish future."

Li, whose company Baidu is one of China's leading AI players, signals this isn't realistic.

Of the 198 participants who signed up for the XPT—a four-month exercise from June through October 2022—169 submitted forecasts. # Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament

Forecasting Existential Risks: Evidence from a Long-Run Forecasting Tournament [...] The Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) aimed to produce high-quality forecasts of the risks facing humanity over the next century by incentivizing thoughtful forecasts, explanations, persuasion, and updating from 169 forecasters over a multi-stage tournament. In this first iteration of the XPT, we discover points where historically accurate forecasters on short-run questions (superforecasters) and domain experts agree and disagree in their probability estimates of short-, medium-, and [...] What are the gravest risks facing humanity over the next century and beyond? In 2022, the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) brought together 80 experts and 89 superforecasters to predict the risks to humanity posed by artificial intelligence, nuclear war, pandemics, and other causes.

results.title: Will AI kill us? Superforecasters and experts disagree
results.content:
To collect predictions about high-stakes existential risks, the Forecasting Research Institute asked a total of 169 superforecasters, AI experts, and experts in other fields to predict the likelihood of different disasters occurring over various timeframes: 2024, 2030, 2050, and 2100. The participants submitted predictions individually and in groups, and were offered incentives, including cash prizes, to encourage engagement.

a table with a number of different numbers. [...] Subscribe now

What are the odds that AI will kill humanity by 2100? That was one of the many questions asked in the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament, held by the Forecasting Research Institute. The contest collected predictions from technical experts and “superforecasters” (people with a track record of making accurate predictions) about various existential threats — ranging from AI to nuclear war to pandemics.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: Forecasts are grounded in base rates of natural and anthropogenic catastrophes, adjusted for emerging technological risks, and heavily informed by the Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT) results. Total extinction risk by 2100 is estimated at 2.5%, reflecting a blend of superforecaster (1%) and expert (6%) consensus, with AI (1.5%) as the primary driver, followed by engineered pandemics (0.2%) and nuclear war (0.05%). Lower severity thresholds (e.g., ≥1k, ≥100k) are dominated by natural disasters and conventional conflicts, approaching 100% for 'Total' risk over longer horizons. AI risk scales steeply over time as capabilities advance, while nuclear risk remains relatively flat due to established deterrence mechanisms. Biological risks are elevated by the increasing accessibility of genetic engineering, though state and non-state actor capabilities are differentiated. All probabilities strictly adhere to logical constraints: non-decreasing over time, non-increasing with severity, and respecting subset/superset relationships across causes and thresholds.

results.title: Covid-19 Fatality Rate
results.content: The 1% case fatality rate of COVID-19 can be thought of as the running percentage of COVID-19 cases that have resulted in death. It doesn’t represent the true average probability of death, though, since the virus, and the global population’s immunity and behavior, have changed so much over time. The conditions are not constant. [...] The biological process of a disease leading to death is complex and uncertain. It is unpredictable and therefore random. Each person has a real physical risk of dying from COVID-19, though this risk varies over time and place and between individuals. So, at best, 1% could be the average probability of death within the population. [...] Case fatality rate is a probability, but only when you look at the specific data set it was directly calculated from. If you were to write the outcome of every COVID-19 case in that data set on a strip of paper and randomly select one from a hat, you have a 1% chance of selecting a case that ended in death. Doing this only for cases from a particular group, such as a group of older adults with a higher risk or young children with a lower risk, would cause the percentage to be higher or lower.

label: Gemini 3.1 Pro
rationale: The historical base rate of pandemics killing >1% of the global population (e.g., the 1918 influenza) suggests an annual probability of roughly 0.1% to 0.3%. However, modern medical countermeasures (rapid mRNA vaccines, antivirals, antibiotics for secondary infections) significantly reduce the likelihood of a natural pathogen reaching this mortality threshold today, despite increased global connectivity. In the 2022 Existential Risk Persuasion Tournament (XPT), superforecasters estimated the risk of a non-genetically-engineered pathogen killing >1% of humans at 0.5% by 2030, 1.69% by 2050, and 3.63% by 2100. Given that we are now in late 2026, the window for a qualifying 5-year period ending by 2030 is very narrow, reducing the near-term probability to around 0.3%. For 2050 and 2100, I align closely with the XPT superforecaster medians (1.5% and 4%, respectively), balancing the persistent threat of zoonotic spillovers (like H5N1) against continued advancements in biosurveillance and medical technology.

Pandemics — especially engineered pandemics — pose a significant risk to humanity. [...] Thankfully, few people seek to use disease as a weapon, and even those willing to conduct such attacks may not aim to produce the most harmful pathogen possible. The risk might be especially high during great power conflicts.

rationale: Only one natural pathogen in the last two centuries (1918 flu) killed >1% of humanity within 5 years, and COVID-19—despite being a major modern pandemic—killed only ~0.2-0.35%, a factor of 3-5 below the threshold, suggesting modern medicine substantially truncates the tail. results.title: Explaining international differences in excess mortality due to Covid-19 | Scientific Reports

label: GPT-5.5
rationale: The base rate for pandemics killing >1% of humanity is very low in the modern era: 1918 flu likely qualifies, while COVID-19’s ~15 million estimated excess deaths in 2020–21 was far below the ~80 million threshold, and most post-1918 influenza pandemics were far smaller. Current H5N1 circulation and continued zoonotic/lab-escape risks keep the tail non-negligible, but as of mid-2026 human cases remain rare with no sustained human-to-human spread, and vaccines, antivirals, surveillance, and rapid platform technologies should usually prevent natural pathogens from reaching 1918-scale global mortality. I put weight on historical base rates adjusted downward for modern medicine but upward for global connectivity and expert/XPT estimates, yielding a slowly accumulating hazard rather than a near-zero risk.

results.content:
Humans face unprecedented peril from new technologies and from our own actions, according to a new book by Toby Ord. By Ord's reckoning, humanity has a 1-in-6 chance of suffering an existential catastrophe this century.

Why it matters:The sheer havoc COVID-19 has caused to our globally connected economy and our clear failure to prepare for such a low-probability but high-consequence threat doesn't bode well for a future where existential risk will intensify. [...] Toby Ordis a moral philosopher at Oxford University, where he focuses on existential risk — catastrophes so huge they could plausibly threaten the future of humanity. His new book, "The Precipice: Existential Risk and the Future of Humanity," explores why that risk is on the rise and what we can do in this moment of danger to safeguard our future. [...] — Toby Ord, Oxford University
The big picture:While we may picture world-ending threats in the form of an incoming asteroid or something similarly cosmic, Ord's view is that the much bigger dangers are the risks humanity introduces into the world: nuclear war, climate change, bioengineered pandemics and out-of-control AI.

In The Precipice, I gave my best guess probabilities for the existential risk over the next 100 years in each of these areas. results.content:
### Scale

Pandemics — especially engineered pandemics — pose a significant risk to humanity. Though the risk is difficult to assess, some researchers estimate that there is a greater than 1 in 10,000 chance of a biological catastrophe leading to human extinction within the next 100 years, and potentially as high as 1 in 100. (See below.) A biological catastrophe that doesn’t lead to extinction could still kill billions of people.

### Neglectedness [...] But despite the horror of these past events, it seems unlikely that a natural pandemic could be bad enough on its own to drive humanity to total extinction in the foreseeable future, given what we know of events in natural history.6

As philosopher Toby Ord argues in his book The Precipice, history suggests humanity faces a very low baseline extinction risk — the chance of being wiped out in ordinary circumstances — from natural causes. [...] But we believe future pandemics may be among the largest contributors to existential risk this century, because it now seems possible that advanced biotechnology is reaching a stage where it could be used to create pandemics that would kill more than 50% of the population — not just in a particular area, but globally. It’s possible they could be bad enough to drive humanity to extinction, or at least cause so much damage that civilisation never recovers.

results.title: Existential Risk - an overview
results.content:
Global catastrophic risks have the potential to cause serious harm on a planetary scale (Bostrom and Cirkovic, 2011). A particularly severe category of global catastrophic risk is an existential risk: one that threatens the premature extinction of earth-originating intelligent life, or the permanent and drastic destruction of its potential for future development (Bostrom, 2013). The key difference is that existential catastrophes curtail the possibility of recovery and future development. [...] Views on how catastrophic and existential risks should be conceptualized differ. Existing research typically focuses on discrete ‘knock out’ events and the direct consequences of these events. Examples include asteroid impacts, supervolcanoes, pandemic outbreaks, the possibly catastrophic consequences of future physics experiments, and the development of artificial superintelligence. [...] The desire to broaden the scope of research in catastrophic and existential risk, and further its connections with other areas of expertise, was a key motivation for both the first Cambridge Conference on Catastrophic Risk and this special issue, which brings together many papers originally presented at that conference. Below, we’ll introduce the papers collected within, and in doing so draw together some common themes and lessons.

results.title: What were the death tolls from pandemics in history?
results.content:
This overview shows us the vast impact that pandemics have had over history.

You can see that the largest pandemics — such as the Black Death — killed more than half of the population. Several pandemics have swept through the population repeatedly: in just the last two hundred years, seven major pandemics were caused by cholera, and another seven were caused by the flu. [...] ## The Black Death

The Black Death (1346–1353 CE) — one of the earliest pandemics with a methodically estimated death toll — killed around 50–60% of Europe’s population, approximately 50 million people, in just 6 years.3

Researchers have established that many people also died elsewhere — as large outbreaks are also recognizable in historical records from Western Asia, the Middle East, and North Africa — but comprehensive estimates of the global death toll are not available. [...] Recent research (Spreeuwenberg et al., 2018) has estimated a global death toll of around 17 million, using excess mortality estimates from high-income countries with high levels of death registration and extrapolating mortality rates to the global population. However, many sources have found higher flu mortality rates in poorer countries, suggesting this is likely underestimated.
